title: Five short nights: how appealing sweets looked to 31 teens [five_nights, final_31]
teaser: Teens spent five nights with 6.5 hours in bed and five with 10, in random order. [five_nights, sr_in_bed, hs_in_bed, randomized_order] After the short nights, they rated photos of sweets and desserts as more appealing. [sweets_more_appealing] Their hunger showed no clear difference. [hunger_ns]
hook: Five nights of 6.5 hours in bed, and teens rated photos of sweets and desserts as more appealing. [five_nights, sr_in_bed, sweets_more_appealing] Their hunger showed no clear difference. [hunger_ns]
populationPanel: Who this was tested in: 31 typically developing teens aged 14 to 17. [final_31, inclusion] 59% were girls; 52% were white and 41% African-American. [female_59, ethnicity] The study left out teens with marked obesity. [exclusion_obesity] Each teen slept at home on both schedules, in an order set by a random draw. [at_home, randomized_order] The result describes teens like these, after five short nights. [final_31, limit_after_five]

card.question: Do short nights make sweets look better to teens? [sweets_more_appealing]
card.headline: After five short nights, teens rated sweets and desserts as more appealing. [five_nights, sweets_more_appealing]
card.support: Hunger and the appeal of other foods showed no clear difference. [hunger_ns, nonsweets_ns]

source.span: five short and five long nights each [five_nights]

glance.alt: Two bars across a night, one for each schedule. [-] On the short nights, sleep starts much later; both bars end at the same wake time. [later_onset, wake_same]
glance.note: Drawn from the paper’s own measurements. [-]
glance.tryIt: compare calories and sweets after each kind of night [-]

paragraphs: Picture a scoreboard in your head that rates each food as it comes into view. [hedonic_shift] The score is how much pleasure the food seems to promise; psychologists call it hedonic value. [hedonic_shift] A higher score makes a food more likely to get eaten. [appeal_to_intake]

The authors' idea is that short sleep turns up the score for sweet things. [hedonic_shift, may_increase_appeal] Earlier work in adults points the same way. [-] Sleep-deprived adults crave calorie-dense food more. [adult_cravings] In brain scans, food photos set off reward areas more after short sleep. [adult_brain]

This trial checked the score in teens. [-] Each teen spent five nights with 6.5 hours in bed and five with 10. [five_nights, sr_in_bed, hs_in_bed] Only the bedtime moved; the wake time stayed the same, weekends included. [bedtime_moved, same_wake] They slept 6.7 hours a night on the short schedule and 9.1 on the long one. [sleep_sr, sleep_hs]

The morning after each block, they rated 84 food photos from “gross” to “delicious”. [photo_sets, rating_scale] Sweets and desserts looked more appealing after the short nights. [sweets_more_appealing] Meat, eggs, fruit and vegetables showed no clear difference. [nonsweets_ns] Neither did hunger. [hunger_ns]

So what moved was how sweets looked; hunger showed no clear difference. [sweets_more_appealing, hunger_ns] The authors see this as one route from short sleep to eating more sweets. [may_increase_appeal]

figure.caption: When the teens fell asleep and woke, on average, under each schedule. [onset_sr, onset_hs, wake_sr, wake_hs]
figure.alt: Two bars across a night. [-] On the short nights, sleep starts at 0:34 and ends at 7:12. [onset_sr, wake_sr] On the long nights, it starts at 22:06 and ends at 7:11. [onset_hs, wake_hs] The bars end together, because only the bedtime moved. [wake_same, bedtime_moved]

paragraphs: The tested schedule: five nights in a row with 10 hours in bed, against five with 6.5 hours. [five_nights, hs_in_bed, sr_in_bed] The wake time stayed fixed every morning, weekends included, so only the bedtime moved. [same_wake, bedtime_moved]

With 10 hours in bed, the teens were asleep by about 22:06 and slept 9.1 hours. [hs_in_bed, onset_hs, sleep_hs] They took no naps and kept caffeine to 1 coffee or energy drink a day. [no_naps_caffeine] The trial measured how appealing food looked, not anyone's health. [primary_appeal]

audit.effect: Teens rated sweet and dessert photos more appealing after short sleep than after healthy sleep: a standardized effect (Cohen’s d) of .41. [sweets_more_appealing, sweets_d] By convention, .20 is small and .50 medium. [d_convention]
audit.weakEnd: The paper reports no confidence interval for this effect. [sweets_more_appealing] Its test gives p = .045 in the abstract and p = .049 in the results. [sweets_p_abstract, sweets_p_results] Both sit just inside the usual line, so the weak end may sit close to zero. [-]
limitations: Small: 31 teens, measured only after five short nights. [limit_small, final_31, limit_after_five]
Hunger was only self-rated, and nobody measured physical activity. [limit_hunger_measure, limit_activity]
The study did not track the menstrual cycle, and the wash-out between schedules lasted 2 days. [limit_menstrual, limit_washout]
audit.missed: Food eaten was only an exploratory check, in 23 teens, with no test reported for this sample. [diet_exploratory, diet_23] Calories were 1860 after short nights against 1647 after long ones. [kcal_sr, kcal_hs] The 52% rise in sweets was 0.74 against 0.49 servings a day. [sweets_more_eaten, sweets_sr, sweets_hs]
more: Pooled with the authors' earlier study, 68 teens ate 1934 kcal against 1764 (p = .039). [pooled_68, pooled_kcal_sr, pooled_kcal_hs, pooled_kcal_p] Sweets: 1.46 against 0.75 servings a day (p = .017). [pooled_sweets_sr, pooled_sweets_hs, pooled_sweets_p]
Sleep per night, by wrist sensor in 28 teens: 6.7 hours short, 9.1 hours long. [sleep_28, sleep_sr, sleep_hs]
Sleep began at 0:34 against 22:06; waking came at 7:12 against 7:11. [onset_sr, onset_hs, wake_sr, wake_hs]
No sign that the first schedule carried over into the second. [no_carryover]
Of 38 randomized, one dropped out and 6 broke the schedule, leaving 31. [randomized_38, dropped_7, final_31]
Each rating left out teens who strongly disliked that food type. [dislikers_removed]
Funded by the US National Institutes of Health, which had no role; no competing interests. [funding, funder_no_role, no_competing]

glossary.plain: How much pleasure a food seems to promise before you eat it.
The average difference between two conditions, divided by how much that difference varied from person to person.
Set by chance, here the order of the two sleep schedules.
Kilocalories, the unit of food energy that labels usually just call calories.

takeaways: After five nights of 6.5 hours in bed, teens rated sweets and desserts as more appealing than after 10-hour nights. [five_nights, sr_in_bed, hs_in_bed, sweets_more_appealing]
Hunger and the appeal of other foods showed no clear difference. [hunger_ns, nonsweets_ns]
The trial was small, and measured only after five short nights. [limit_small, limit_after_five]
